reason: Paper directly characterizes teneurin protein structure and evolution, including the C-terminal domain determined by X-ray crystallography and EM, alternative splicing effects on teneurin diversification, and multifunctional receptor features. TENM3 encodes teneurin-3 (ODZ3/TEN3/KIAA1455), one of the four teneurin family members. Structural characterization of the teneurin scaffold is foundational content for understanding TENM3 biology.

Title unambiguously describes alpha-crystallin complexes (alpha-gamma and alpha-beta) and demonstrates the in vivo chaperone role of alpha-crystallin. CRYAA encodes alphaA-crystallin, the primary alpha-crystallin subunit in the lens. The abstract is empty but the title establishes direct relevance to CRYAA chaperone function, a central feature of the gene.

Paper directly studies alphaA-crystallin (CRYAA) and alphaB-crystallin double-knockout mice to dissect caspase inhibition in lens fiber cell terminal differentiation. Shows that alphaA-crystallin interacts with caspase 6 and suppresses caspase activity to maintain lens fiber cell integrity. This is mechanistic work directly on the CRYAA gene product in the lens.

Directly examines how endogenous metabolites modulate alpha-crystallin anti-aggregation (chaperone) activity using beta-crystallin and alcohol dehydrogenase as substrates. Alpha-crystallin chaperone activity is a defining function of CRYAA; modulation of this activity by physiological compounds is relevant to CRYAA lens biology and cataract susceptibility.

Paper explicitly uses human alphaA-crystallin (CRYAA) and alphaB-crystallin to study how chaperone-client complexes undergo glycation-mediated cross-linking. Shows age-associated increase in AGE-mediated cross-linking correlates with lens stiffness and presbyopia. Directly studies CRYAA protein in the context of lens aging, a phenotype relevant to the gene.

Directly quantifies age-related increase in alpha-, beta-, and gamma-crystallin degradation fragments in human lens high-molecular-weight protein complexes, identifying cleavage sites by N-terminal sequencing. Alpha-crystallin (CRYAA is the major alphaA subunit) fragmentation is directly relevant to CRYAA age-related biology and cataract formation.

Paper directly screens USH1C for mutations in Usher syndrome type 1 patients and non-syndromic deafness families using DHPLC, identifies the 238-239insC mutation and assesses its haplotypic background. USH1C (harmonin) is the ophthalmogenetics gene of interest; Usher syndrome type 1 causes both deafness and retinitis pigmentosa. Directly relevant to USH1C mutation spectrum.

Title explicitly names CRYAA, and the abstract describes systematic investigation of CRYAA expression in in vivo (rabbit naphthalene cataract) and in vitro (HLEB3 H2O2) age-related cataract models. Shows CRYAA silencing increases apoptosis and autophagy in lens epithelial cells. This is direct and primary research on CRYAA in cataract.

Meta-analysis directly investigating three CRYAA promoter polymorphisms (rs3761381, rs13053109, rs7278468) and their association with cataract susceptibility. Finds rs7278468 G allele carriers have significantly decreased cataract risk. This is core CRYAA genetic epidemiology directly tied to the gene's disease association.

Review of developmental macular disorders and their molecular genetic basis. OPN1MW mutations cause blue-cone monochromacy with macular dysfunction, and SLC38A8 mutations cause isolated foveal hypoplasia - both are developmental macular disorders. This review of the category's phenotypes and genetic underpinning is directly relevant to understanding both genes in disease context.

Paper reports that Col18a1-knockout mice develop anterior segment defects including fragile iris, iris adhesion to lens and cornea, posterior pigment epithelial cell defoliation, and ciliary body atrophy. COL18A1 encodes type XVIII collagen; this mouse study directly establishes COL18A1's role in anterior ocular integrity, an important complement to its known role in Knobloch syndrome.

Double knockout mice for collagens XV and XVIII (COL18A1) study is directly about COL18A1 (type XVIII collagen) and reveals lack of functional compensation between these two closely related collagens. While the abstract is absent, the title is unambiguous in relevance to COL18A1.

Clinical case report of amniotic membrane graft for macular hole in a patient with Knobloch syndrome. Knobloch syndrome (KS, MIM 267750) is definitively caused by biallelic mutations in COL18A1. Surgical management of ocular complications in COL18A1-associated Knobloch syndrome is directly relevant to the gene's clinical significance.

Correction letter establishing that a reported case of Knobloch syndrome with apparent ADAMTS18 mutation was, in fact, due to a COL18A1 mutation missed by initial analysis. Includes clinical characterization of KS ocular phenotype (ectopia lentis, cryptless irides, high myopia, vitreoretinal atrophy, macular atrophy). Directly relevant to COL18A1 mutation detection and Knobloch syndrome.

Paper directly studies OPN1LW (human red pigment) and OPN1MW (mouse green pigment) by replacing the mouse X-linked green opsin with the human red opsin gene. Uses multi-electrode array recordings to characterize chromatic sensitivity and retinal ganglion cell responses. Directly relevant to both OPN1LW and OPN1MW biology in cone photoreceptors.

Study of VEP abnormalities in albinism, showing strong correlation between foveal hypoplasia grade and interhemispheric VEP latency asymmetry due to optic nerve misrouting. SLC38A8 mutations cause isolated foveal hypoplasia with optic nerve misrouting and nystagmus - phenotypically identical to albinism's ocular features. This paper characterizes the electrophysiological phenotype of foveal hypoplasia with misrouting, directly informative for SLC38A8-related disease. Link to OPN1MW is indirect (color opsin function is distinct from misrouting phenotype).

Large population review of inherited red-green color deficiency prevalence across ethnicities. Red-green color deficiency is caused by mutations or deletion of OPN1LW and OPN1MW. The prevalence data, population genetics (founder effects, genetic drift) and male:female ratios are directly relevant to the epidemiology of OPN1LW-associated disease.

Directly analyzes OPN1LW molecular variation including the Ser180Ala polymorphism, spectral tuning of red and green cone pigments, hybrid gene formation via unequal recombination, and the red/green gene array structure. OPN1LW encodes the long-wave sensitive cone opsin; this review of its molecular genetics and resulting color vision phenotypes is core content for the gene.

Review of molecular genetics of color vision and color vision defects, discussing OPN1LW (and OPN1MW) gene structure, the tandem array on Xq28, spectral polymorphisms, and mechanisms underlying color deficiency. OPN1LW is directly the subject of this review. Relevant as foundational molecular genetics for the gene.

Paper purifies and characterizes holo-Elongator as a six-subunit complex, discovers Elp4/Elp5/Elp6 subcomplex, and clones the human homologue of ELP4, showing it is ubiquitously expressed. ELP4 is the gene of interest (associated with aniridia/anterior segment dysgenesis via its location in the PAX6 locus). This paper defines ELP4's protein function as an Elongator subunit and establishes the human gene, making it directly relevant.
